<reason>A (CON) controlled the debate's structure with the slogan-or-teeth dilemma pressed from Rebuttal 1 onward. When B finally named teeth in Rebuttal 2 (export duties, diverted megawatts, pulled rail), A converted them into concrete harms — lower farmgate prices, cross-border cocoa smuggling, taxing the forex-earning base to fund uncompetitive factories — that B's closing never addressed. A's precedent question (name one country that industrialized selling mainly to neighbors as poor as itself) was never answered with an example; B's "Korea had Japan" partially conceded A's geometry point about purchasing power. B's Botswana flip was the single best turn of the debate and its jobs frame stayed live, but A engaged it directly (uncompetitive factories hire nobody; jobs lost twice), while B left A's late incidence analysis untouched. A's closing crystallized the clash ("slogan or self-harm"; "a market you must build is a market you do not have on the day the megawatt moves") more decisively than B's reassertion. A's clipped Rebuttal 2 is a small execution cost, outweighed by its structural command.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive chain: A's Q1 forced B to name real trade-offs; B's A1 obliged with differential export duties and diverted power/rail; A's Rebuttal 2 then turned those very instruments against B — export duties cut farmgate prices and invite the smuggling West African cocoa is known for, taxing the certain earner to subsidize the speculative one. B's closing reasserted "factories hire" without ever answering that critique of its own named teeth.</best_rebuttal>
